newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Taylor extends lead in Liberian election.
newsitem.headline: Taylor extends lead in Liberian election.

text.p: Former warlord Charles Taylor extended his lead in Liberia's elections on Monday, edging towards a victory through the ballot box that he failed to achieve by the gun.
Election Commission chief Harry Andrews said that with one third of potential votes counted, Taylor had just under 66 percent of valid votes cast, up from 62 percent on Sunday.
Taylor's closest rival, former senior U.N. official Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, the only woman in the field of 12, saw her tally fall from 18 percent to less than 16 percent.

And as early results showed Taylor's lead widening, Johnson- Sirleaf headed off tension by toning down her charges of poll fraud. She told her supporters to prepare for the role of "a strong and constructive opposition" if it came to that.

"Should it come to us becoming an opposition party in this country we must remain a strong and constructive opposition, that is working towards helping our people return to normal lives," she said to cheers from supporters packing her party headquarters.

Acknowleding that weighty international observers had emphatically endorsed the conduct of the poll, Johnson-Sirleaf said her Unity Party would await fuller accounts from its polling agents before passing judgment on its credibility.
Earlier Johnson-Sirleaf said unauthorised people helped some voters.
"People did not know how to vote in many areas and needed assistance. During that assistance their intent and wishes were not respected," she told state radio.
Former U.S. president Jimmy Carter said most problems his team had seen stemmed from general ignorance on how to vote.
"These problems or irregularities did not have a pattern and did not affect the outcome of the elections," he said.
Taylor needs 50 percent plus to avoid an August 2 run-off.
With 219,754 votes counted, Taylor had 144,981 or 65.97 percent. Johnson-Sirleaf had 34,914 or 15.88 percent.

Taylor supporters remained calm on Monday, in contrast to Sunday night when the announcement of the first preliminary results provoked chants of "Taylor has won" across the capital. Taylor's National Patriotic Party ordered its followers to hold off partying until final results were proclaimed.
Andrews said some 600,000 cast ballots from about 700,000 registered to vote.
Taylor is seen by many as the forceful leader needed in the post-war period. He had superior resources to his rivals. With a national radio station, he ran a well-oiled campaign machine.
Johnson-Sirleaf entered the race late but built up support through her image of integrity and good contacts with donors.
Two other former warlords, Alhaji Kromah and George Boley, also ran. Kromah was in third place with 4.29 percent.
Liberia's West African neighbours, who finally rallied the warlords around a peace deal, earlier joined the international observers in praising the smooth conduct of the poll.
